deep.reconstruction: This page continues the editorial summary (Summarium) that precedes E296 in Novi Commentarii Academiae Petropolitanae vol. 10. It is historical and programmatic, with no computation. It runs from the Bernoulli brothers to Euler's own work. Johann Bernoulli later made up for the shortcomings of his isoperimetric method. Long afterwards Euler (the 'Auctor') reduced all such problems to one form: find a curve y(x) that makes a functional J[y] = ∫V dx a maximum or minimum. Here V may be any expression in x and y, in their differentials of any order (dy/dx, d²y/dx², …), and even in further integral formulas ∫Z dx. These last make the integrand nonlocal (Euler's 'formulae integrales indeterminatae', as in Methodus inveniendi, 1744, ch. 3). Measured against this standard, the Bernoulli solutions are limited in two ways. They cover only V depending on first-order differentials. They exclude integrands containing integral formulas, except a few cases that can easily be transformed away. Euler filled these gaps both in the Commentarii papers and in the 1744 monograph. He nevertheless found his own method 'not natural enough'. Its whole force rested on considering the elements of the curve (varying single ordinates, i.e. a discretised polygonal approach). The question itself, by contrast, can be posed purely analytically, separated from geometry. The next page continues: Lagrange, using analysis alone (δ-method, 1755 letter / Miscellanea Taurinensia 1762), obtained the same solution. This led Euler to found the 'calculus variationum'.

ideas.modern_name: General one-dimensional variational problem with higher-order and nonlocal (integro-differential) Lagrangians
